heading: Models: types without a role
body: Data types that several files share live in client/models/ or server/models/. A models folder is not a role folder. A models file holds data, not behavior (ADR 0041, ADR 0043). Choose a language below. TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, C#, F#, Dart, Kotlin, Go, Java, Ruby and Lua models work in both realms. A JavaScript models file holds one JSDoc `@typedef` comment and `export {}`, such as `client/models/CartTotal.js` for `CartTotal`. Every JavaScript file of the realm uses a JavaScript model by its name, with no import. JavaScript also reads the TypeScript models of its realm: write `/** @import { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts' */` above the class. Routes, events and `/api.json` read these models like the models of any other language. A `@typedef` in another JavaScript file of client/ or server/ is a model outside its folder. `ty migrate fix --write` moves it to the models folder. It keeps one file for identical copies. When a copy matches a model that the realm already has, in JavaScript or TypeScript, the fix removes the copy and imports that model. It reports a copy that differs, and leaves that file for you. The build refuses an inline `@typedef` with `TY1310`; `ty migrate fix --write` moves it into the models folder. Swift models live only in client/models/, because Swift is not a Yon language. Python and PHP models live only in server/models/, because those languages run only in Yon. So their example, like the Java one, is a route that returns the guide, and the page is not part of it. A controller returns a model, or takes one with FromBody, and Yon turns it into JSON and back, like Spring. A PHP array has no item type, so a doc comment gives it: `/** @var list<Guide> */` on a property, or `@param list<Guide> $guides` and `@return list<Guide>` on a controller method. A TypeScript models file holds interfaces, type aliases and import type statements. TypeScript removes a type-only import, so the browser never loads the models file. In the other languages, a models file holds structs, records, data classes, enums and type aliases with fields only. It also holds the imports they need. Every models file holds one model: one interface, type alias, JSDoc `@typedef`, struct, record, class, enum or Ruby record, and the file is named after it, such as `Guide.ts` for `Guide` (ADR 0067). Put a second model, even a small enum, in both realms, so their tab shows the service that the page reads and a route that returns the same guide. A JavaScript models file holds one type, because Tachyon compiles it as another file of the program's package main. The framework adds the realm's models files of that language to every program it builds in that language. It never routes a models file and never ships one on its own. A Rust model declares its type and fields pub, because the models files become the module crate::models. A role annotation in a models folder fails with TY1310. The message names the role folder where the type belongs. A method, a function, a constant or a service marker also fails with TY1310. So does any other statement, or a language in another JavaScript file of client/ or server/ is a model outside its folder. `ty migrate fix --write` moves it to the models folder. It keeps one file for identical copies. When a copy matches a model that the realm already has, in JavaScript or TypeScript, the fix removes the copy and imports that model. It reports a copy that differs, and leaves that file for you. The build refuses an inline `@typedef` with `TY1310`; `ty migrate fix --write` moves it into the models folder. Swift models live only in client/models/, because Swift is not a Yon language. Python, PHP, Groovy and Lua models live only in server/models/, because those languages run only in Yon. So their example is only a route that returns the guide, and the page is not part of it. A controller returns a model, or takes one with FromBody, and Yon turns it into JSON and back, like Spring. A PHP array has no item type, so a doc comment gives it: `/** @var list<Guide> */` on a property, or `@param list<Guide> $guides` and `@return list<Guide>` on a controller method. A TypeScript models file holds interfaces, type aliases and import type statements. TypeScript removes a type-only import, so the browser never loads the models file. In the other languages, a models file holds structs, records, data classes, enums and type aliases with fields only. It also holds the imports they need. Every models file holds one model: one interface, type alias, JSDoc `@typedef`, struct, record, class, enum or Ruby record, and the file is named after it, such as `Guide.ts` for `Guide` (ADR 0067). Put a second model, even a small enum, in its own file next to the first. A models file with two models fails with `TY1318`, and `ty migrate fix --write` splits it into one file per model. Other files import a model in the usual way of their language: `import type { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts'`, `use crate::models::Guide;`, `using Models;`, `import 'models/Guide.dart';`, `import models.Guide`, `import models.Guide;`, `open Models`, `from models import Guide` or `use Models\Guide;`. JavaScript, Swift, Go, Ruby and Lua use the type name with no import. A Ruby model is a Data.define record whose fields have YARD @!attribute types. A Lua model is a table whose fields have `---@field` types. A Go models file holds one type, because Tachyon compiles it as another file of the program's package main. The framework adds the realm's models files of that language to every program it builds in that language. It never routes a models file and never ships one on its own. A Rust model declares its type and fields pub, because the models files become the module crate::models. Each Rust models file is its own module inside it, so a model that uses another model writes `use crate::models::Item;`. When a models file does not compile, the error names that file. A role annotation in a models folder fails with TY1310. The message names the role folder where the type belongs. A method, a function, a constant or a service marker also fails with TY1310. So does any other statement, or a language in the wrong realm.
